description: Our mission is to help humans live and work safely on Mars. With diverse skills across food and nutrition, artificial intelligence, software development, embedded systems, IoT, cybersecurity and data processing, our team from Uganda is trying to solve the problem of how astronauts can navigate, communicate and survive on foot where there is no GPS, no compass and no quick help from Earth.
summary:
URGUIDE is a web-based Mars surface guide for astronauts on a Marswalk. It puts real NASA data into one map, a first-person helmet display and a top-view planner. The demo is set near Jezero Crater, northeast of the Perseverance landing site.

The challenge asks for a layered map for one surface excursion, built from several NASA missions, with a route and a focus on astronaut safety. URGUIDE does this at walking scale. It layers MOLA/HRSC elevation, CTX imagery, thermal inertia, dust and slope on a 200 m grid. The astronaut sets the landing zone and target, or draws a route through chosen points, and sees where the route is safe. The planner also gives an EVA resource budget, a live elevation profile, vitals, rover status, and relay nodes that show radio coverage, plus live safety alerts such as dust storms and a help signal.

This matters because Mars has no GPS and no compass, the horizon is only about 3.4 km away, and a message to Earth takes minutes. A crew needs navigation, communications and safety information that works locally, and needs to see how far they can safely go before they leave.
details:
What does your project do and how does it work?
URGUIDE helps astronauts plan and carry out a walk on Mars. A Python script cuts NASA GeoTIFFs onto a metre grid and writes one data file, and a web page reads it. The grid holds the USGS MOLA-HRSC 200 m elevation model, the Murray Lab CTX image mosaic, thermal inertia and a dust cover index. In the top-view planner, the user sets the start and target by clicking the map or typing coordinates, and can draw a route through their own points. The app finds a safe path over the real slopes and suggests smooth landing zones near the target. It then prices the route in suit consumables, time and rover battery for both walking and rover travel. The helmet display shows what is left, what it will take to reach the target or return to the landing zone, arrival times, a turn-back point and a walk-back test in case the rover fails. The app also places relay nodes around the landing zone and along the route and shows signal reach over the real terrain, including the planet’s curvature. In first person, the astronaut can look around 360°, sees pointers to base, nodes, the target and named places such as Jezero, and watches a live elevation profile, vitals and rover health. A dust front triggers a red blinking display with its direction, speed and arrival time, and the Help button sends the astronaut’s position through the nodes to the base with a rescue time estimate.

What benefit does it have?
It lets a crew or mission planner test a surface plan before and during a walk. They can see whether it fits the budget, whether it stays within radio reach, and what to do in an emergency.

What is the intended impact?
We want human exploration of Mars to be safer and better planned by giving future crews decision support at walking scale, and to show how existing NASA data can be combined for that purpose. The same approach could be used at other landing sites and on the Moon.

What tools did you use?
The 3D terrain and helmet display are built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Three.js. Python with NumPy, Rasterio and Pillow, together with GDAL, processes the data. We developed in VS Code with AI assistance from Claude. The data comes from the USGS and NASA MOLA-HRSC blended elevation model, the Murray Lab global CTX mosaic, TES thermal inertia and dust cover index layers from NASA’s Mars Trek, and the IAU planetary nomenclature for place names.

How is your project creative?
It joins three things that are usually kept apart: a map of real terrain, a first-person helmet view, and a live model of resources and communications. Radio coverage is part of route planning, so a route turns red where the crew would lose signal. The budget rejects plans that look fine on a map, and the astronaut gets one view to use during the walk, not several separate tools.

What factors did your team consider?
Astronaut safety came first, which is why the app includes turn-back and walk-back rules, vitals, alerts and a help signal. We were careful with data, labelling on screen and in the credits what is real, what is computed from real data, and what is simulated or assumed. We also considered the limits of suits and a rover, the short horizon, curvature, the lack of GPS and the delay to Earth, and we made the tool easy to use by letting the astronaut choose the target, route, nodes and simulation speed.
